For ELEC and other non-CPEG students, if you are not very passionate on robotics AND have much experience such as robotics team, DONT TAKE THIS COURSE. Take other co-op projects or do fyp rather. You will definitely regret from enrolling this course.

This course introduce basic ideas of embedded system, also labs for basic embedded system. At last will have a project for STM32.

I learned nothing from this course. I hate embedding system and don't want this in my future career. Proved this course is not a must in CPEG curriculum.

Those are the topics
- Basics of embedded systems, polling and interrupts, number representation etc.
COMP3511 used a half lecture to cover interrupt, but here kaml used 2 lectures for interrupt, we still need to attend it because of the iprs...
- Basic computer structure
- Embedded system structure
- LCD
- Timer
- ADC (Analog-Digital Converter), Motor Interface
- DMA (Direct Memory Access)
- Serial Communication (UART, I2C communication protocols)
- Memory Interface

Sorry to say my strong resentment to this course and kaml makes me feel totally not interested in those topics. I don't know whether is useful in cpeg, or in robotics, maybe is fundamental? Just said that all cpeg students must take this >.<.
sections.grading:
I am a desperate CPEG guy, I must take this course nooooooooo
Huge rant!!!真係好不滿成個grading scheme，要逐個逐個complain

I would like to ask, except the final report, which of the grading component is normal or reasonable???

Passing requirements of the course is
1. Attend all the 6 laboratory experiments with demonstration
2. Attend Interim demonstration AND Final Demonstration
3. Total score > 45%
4. Attend the discussion lecture, which is the sharing to your project ideas to your classmates.

Continuous assessment: (45%)
– In-class activities 8%
Pop-up in class iprs quizzes. Open book open notes open discussions. But what the hell you put some stupid questions that either you directly discussed in class, or can search from the notes.
First, kaml's teaching progress is much slower than lab progress, he almost start the corresponding topics at least 1 weeks AFTER that lab. Also, the lecture contents are extremely theoretical, which is totally useless in the final project!!!
So what is the point to lock in your lectures? THOSE ARE MEANINGLESS
Also, some unreasonable events happened for the iprs quizzes. Once kaml started iprs quizzes SHARPLY after the lectures, without advance notifying, which means if you are late due to transportation or live remote, you will definitely lose the score, especially for some semesters with 9am or 1030am classes.

In some lecture kaml already did iprs questions in the middle and suddenly added iprs at the last second. This is also very annoying which means I cannot early leave and listen his useless lectures.

Some even more FUCKED events regarding iprs during the last lecture of my semester -- Kaml EXPLICITLY told us he will skip iprs questions in the last chapter. But eventually, he RESTARTS the iprs for asking open-ended questions -- which topics you familiar most and not familiar most!!! He WENT TOO FAR, FUCKING, HE WAS JUST LYING!!! 出爾反爾言而無信！！！

Yes, you need to waste 3 hours to listen all the lectures per week. The questions are easy and stupid? You still must lock in, because lab tests will ask you about lecture contents...

– 1 Homework assignment 4%
This part just do simulation about computer arithmetic in COMP2611/ELEC2350 by using STM32, but fox will use some computer program to check your answers in txt file, so you must strictly follow the instructions, otherwise many marks will be deducted.

– 6 Laboratory experiments 15%
This I also need to blame as much!!!
Lab grading is strict and tedious, any late demo will be counted.
Each lab worths 10 marks, 9 marks for demo, 1 mark for bonus if can finish within 90 mins.

Lab 1 is about basic circuits, you can find a labmate (not necessary your project teamate). No any prelab. The time is extremely tedious. Many groups cannot even finish demo, only 5 groups got the bonus score.

Lab 2-6 allow pre-lab, can finish all the tasks before the lab session. But the tasks are difficult and troublesome.

Some tasks are extremely pointless but time-consuming.
In lab3, you need to display your Chinese last name pixel by pixel (>= 24x24) into LCD board... If you are foreign students, please check your last 2 digit card and find its corresponding Chinese character in the university song (last semester refer to the n-th elements in the periodic table). The only function is that you can use draw line function.

Also you need to display 0-359 degree for a compass to LCD, 0-4095 for Analog Digital Converter... Display all values, other cannot pass the demo.

The grading is very strict, Fox and other TAs will ask you how to implement the tasks and further knowledge, you can pass demo only you can finish tasks and answer their questions.

– 1 Preliminary proposal discussion (peer) 3%
This part is just like giving free marks, but totally meaningless. You must attend one lecture to discuss your project idea with your classmates. Then write around 120 words comments to EACH of your 3 other classmates, then you will receive their comments, comment their comments. Then you will get 3% overall.

That lecture is your passing requirement, kaml and fox will show some previous projects and give you iprs to grade them. Then give you their true scores. I think they actually they want us to absolutely obey their grading scheme, although many blemishes and highly subjective...Here are some summary
-If you reuse lab exercise as final project, you must be failed (like getting 6/40).
-If you cannot fully understand the idea behind your product, you will be downgraded (A big wheel with LCD, also many functions about safety box, only got 23.33/40, which only on the mean).
-Grading standard is very high, but ambiguous, you don't know what they like. I know kaml's expectation is extremely high, whose for competition products are the only can get A-range.
-Only STM32 functions will be graded, otherwise like software techniques and bluetooth will not be counted towards the final demo grade.

– 1 Laboratory Test 15%
FUCKKKKKKKKK. Kaml want us to lock in lectures, then he deliberately added this part PARTICULARLY starting from our semester. Just want us to lock in in that bullshit lectures! What is the questions? Ask you what the type of STM32. Mainly lab tasks such as calculating values and compass angle. Also some memorization question based on lecture contents. The questions are like iprs, stupid and easy. So the mean was high.
Mean: 46.4/64
SD: 14.05

The situation become worse. Kaml wants to do normalization because of high mean and fails more people. In Spring 2026, every wrong question will be -0.4*question_scores. This is extremely disgusting!!!
dklm死kaml，特登今年加lab test就係想我地lock in你啲狗屎垃圾堂。今個sem聽講仲話答錯倒扣分，真係好噁心🤮

Project assessment: (55%)
– 1 Proposal presentation 4%
– 1 Interim project demonstration 6%
– 1 Final project demonstration and presentation 40%
– 1 Final project report 5%
For presentation assignments. There will be at least 5 graders including kaml and fox. And your final score will be the maximum of 2 schemes.
In my semester, N = 5
Scheme A: Average for all N graders
Scheme B: Excluding the maximum and minimum scores and take average of middle scores.
Final score = Maximum of Scheme A and Scheme B
One group shares same scores

For example: 5 graders give your group with following marks:
40 30 29 28 10
Scheme A: (40 + 30 + 29 + 28 + 10) / 5 = 27.4
Scheme B: (30 + 29 + 28) / 3 = 29
Final score = Max(27.4, 29) = 29

Kaml said taking maximum makes us feel more fair, but...

For the proposal presentation, we just need to yapping what we want to do in the final project, not necessary that we need to implement everything at the last. But the grading is very subjective, some TAs cannot understand everything and ask stupid questions that how to implement some functions and leave it as excuse to deduct our scores. The grading is even stupid, abstract.

For the interim demo presentation, kaml wants us to show our project progress and do some demonstration. He said that he only wants us to start the project earlier and he "doesn't" require us to implement everything, "doesn't".
But what the fuck the grading is so strict and unreasonable. They deduct our group score into -0.5 SD because of exceeding time limit by 2 second, also "blame" us that our robot cannot move very robustly. They just want us to finish the product in the first 2 weeks... This is very unreasonable!
Mean: 3.98/6
SD: 1.25

What the fuck why all of your comments are very similar? ALL of the markers just stated us "watch your time", "test product limit" Fox listed out our "common mistakes" and what the fuck they just matched of our presentation to the common mistakes list that they prepared at the beginning!!! What the fuck are you doing classification instead of grading???

Personally suspect the fairness of the grading, it is impossible that most of graders have EXACTLY SAME comments and marks. I suspect that kaml gives the grade and comments first then everyone just follows his grading. Whether taking maximum is "fair" again? But kaml one guy can control all the scores. This is stupid.

For final presentation, don't use AI or other assistant. Should finish everything by yourselves. They will ask you deep questions how you implement details. If you cannot answer then you will get very low score. We totally fried...
Mean: 24.233
SD: 9.146

The final assignment is final report. You just need to submit everything that you make before such as project code, presentation ppt, proposal presentation video, etc. Read all requirements line by line. You can get that 5% easily. This assignment is the only normal assignment term throughout this kam course.

Final grading is bad. Given ELEC courses usually maximizes AB range. But kaml maximized CD range. A-range is much less than 25%. Also I know some friends in robotic team said that kaml usually maximized D-range to around 10%.
My friend got almost full in lab test (59/64) and below mean a little bit in final project (20/40). All other components almost full. He overall score 70+ but ended with B- only. This shows kaml's maximized C-range and the overall grading is bad.

This course is very difficult to get good grade. Based on "abnormal" assignment, "unfair" grading and bad grade distribution.  On the other hand, many robotics dudes go this course to boom fish and they already prepare everything during holidays, they have already occupied all A-range which will be disadvantage for all of us, CPEG guys...

夫某人狂悖無度，行若黑社之魁，眾皆不齒。乃強人以名之末字，無漢字可用，必以元素週期表之文逐一顯示，誠為怪誕。又設突擊測驗以逼人聽其空談，雖已託友人傳授 access code，猶於課終復加一題，令人憤懣。

又觀其講授之序，荒誕更甚。課堂進度，遠落於實驗之後——實驗已行一週，狂人方啟其端。所授內容，空懸高論，於final project無半寸之用。然彼自知其言無用，乃於本學期增設實驗筆試，專考課堂所講。於是諸生雖百般不願，亦不得不枯坐三時，聽其虛辭。問之：「此與project何干？」曰：「無干，然吾考之。」問之：「此與實驗何補？」曰：「不補，然吾計分。」此非教書，實為勒贖。

更有甚者，終堂之際，空言二十分，旋稱取消 IPRS 測驗，使人徒費光陰，不知所為何益。及將散未散之時，忽又出爾反爾，回馬一問 IPRS 開放之題，問人何者最熟、何者最疏，真可謂愚妄之至。

嗟乎！此等荒誕之事，眾人皆耳熟能詳也，一日狂人於已時辦學堂，始堂之際瞬即設IPRS測驗，不視天下車水馬龍，不思山中路遠車疏。威迫芸芸學子五更雞啼之時離臥，千里迢迢及學府，凡有為時已晚者，隨即飽受扣分之災。

嗚呼！狂人之行，可謂罄竹難書。本學期更以實驗筆試挾持、以倒扣虐眾、以虛諾欺人。堂堂學府，竟容此輩高坐講台，豈非怪哉？故再申前誡：凡我同窗，見狂人之名，當如避蛇蠍；若不慎入其彀中，則宜默禱其忘開IPRS、忘設倒扣、忘增實驗筆試。若彼一不忘，則諸生唯有咬牙切齒，自求多福。

然此猶未足盡其狂也。近者，狂人更以「常態化分數」為名，陰行屠戮之實。見諸生分數尚可，心生不悅，乃立新規：凡實驗筆試中錯一題，倒扣零點四倍其題分。噫！尋常測驗，錯則失分而已；今狂人設法，錯則倒扣。若題十分，答錯者非但不得，反失四分；連錯三題，本金盡沒，入不敷出。名曰「常態」，實則「地獄」。昔有苛政猛於虎，今見狂人狠於賊。

然吾輩不可徒受其辱。當記其劣跡，廣傳於後世，使後來者知此狂人名號，望風而逃。並聯名具陳，上書學府，請除此害。若終不得伸，則共嘆一句：「狂人之課，丙減猶榮，吾不入地獄，誰入地獄？」悲夫！若非電腦工程書生，逢見狂人即逃之百里，切記切記。
For each lab, I felt extremely terrifying. The Labs are very time consuming and tedious, which takes 2-3 days per lab. Also the extensive time scheduling for 6 labs in 6 consecutive weeks are extremely stressful, which makes me totally outburst and don't want to pay more effort into the lab test and the project...

Also, based on the extent of "abnormal" of assignments term that I mentioned before. This course is very difficult to manage to get very good grade. There are some rumours that getting A-range need spend 3 days 3 nights for final project, is true... We used 1 day 1 night still fried. Cannot imagine how huge workload this course is.

As the other reviewers have mentioned this thousands of times, I will not go through in detail.

Basically in the lectures, you will learn the basic concepts and features of embedded systems such as interrupts, timers, communication protocols etc. The only reason to attend the lectures is to do the IPRS.

Requires solid amount of C programming knolwedge to do the labs and the course project.

We are using STM32F013VET6 as the lab/project MCU (though you can switch to different board for your project needs).

Group project is 2-3ppl. At the first month, you have to come up with the project idea, and you can improve it based on a mandatory peer discussion session concerning complexity and creativity. You then have to create a proposal video on finalized group project title.

On the 2nd month, you will start to do your project. Course will reimburse 120HKD per student to buy things for your project. There is a graded intermin demo to show your project progress. The final demo is basically showcasing your end product and explain your methodology of implementation.

While the lecture content only teach you conceptual stuff. The tutorial does it better as you will have the how to deal with the lab  assignment (and hardware debugging)

Project is the hardest thing in the course. It can be very bad if you got worse groupmates or don't have enoguth time to complete. Recommend taking this course in your final sememster.

sections.content:
The whole course is separated into 2 parts, teaching period and project period.  

**Teaching Period (Week 1 to ~Week 8)**
During teaching period, the following topics will be covered during lectures.

- Basics of embedded systems, polling and interrupts, number representation etc.
- Basic computer structure
- Embedded system structure
- LCD
- Timer
- ADC (Analog-Digital Converter), Motor Interface
- DMA (Direct Memory Access)
- Serial Communication (UART, I2C communication protocols)
- Memory Interface

In addition, you will be greeted with everyone's "favorite" iPRS every lecture.  The timings of iPRS are irregular (eg some are at the start of the class, some are at the end of class).  However you can kinda guess when the iPRS will be held by scanning the lecture notes ahead of time (there will be a page saying iPRS).
As for the tutorials, FOX will give you a briefing on how to do the labs. I highly recommend you to start the labs as soon as possible, do NOT wait until the lab sessions to do them (you most likely won't be able to finish them and get the bonus in time).

Towards the end of the teaching period, the TAs will share what they did for their 3300 project, FYP or how embedded systems are used to solve real-world problems.  Note that, in general, each lecture will have 2 TAs presenting, and each TA will have around 5 iPRS questions.  Which means there are 10 iPRS questions per lecture!!!  In other words, it's fine to skip some of Tim's lecture (which average around 3-5 iPRS questions per lecture) but NEVER skip the TAs presentation.

After the teaching period ends, there will be no more lectures, tutorials and labs.  

**Project Period (~Week 8 to Week 13)**
Lab sessions will be converted into "Help me TA, I'm stuck :/" sessions where you can borrow lab equipment or ask TAs for help.

At around week 4, FOX will hold the first official lecture where he discusses how the project will be graded (rubrics) as well as showcase some previous student's projects and comments on them.

Side note, the course uses C Language.  So make sure you have brushed up on your C skills.

- 1 Final project demo + presentation (40%)
- 1 Final project report (5%)

Note 1: Attending the discussion is a passing requirement

sections.workload:
Oh lord, here we go...

There are mainly 3 components which contribute to having a heavy workload (If I could give -∞ as the "grade" for workload, I would).
(1) Labs are not easy
(2) Overly complex requirements for submissions
(3) Project

**(1) Labs are not easy**
Although FOX will run you through the labs during tutorials, he will NOT give you the answer.  He will only say what is happening for the labs (so that you aren't puzzled when you read the incomprehensible lab handout) as well as the requirements for it.  Copying labs from previous students isn't easy either, as FOX needs you to set your values according to your SID.  

**(2) Overly complex requirements for submissions**
For homework 1, FOX will use an auto-grader for grading the assignment.  The auto-grader isn't ZINC but a custom project written by FOX himself.  It takes in a .txt file and uses string comparison to check for correctness.  In other words, if your format isn't correct, no marks, no appeal :D.
In addition, FOX will also require you to make a PowerPoint and record a presentation video (camera on) for the proposal presentation, 1 minute demo video for final demo and an HTML file which contains every document previously submitted regarding your project.  

**(3) Project**
Disclaimer, both my teammate and I are NOT robotics team.  We are the unfortunate CPEG guys.

The following is my suggestion for the project (it's also what I did).

First and foremost, please for the sake of your own sanity, find a friend, who is responsible and capable, to take this course with you.  Next, think of a topic for your project as early on as possible.  The topic of your project needs to use most of the topics covered in the lectures in a natural way.  Natural meaning the feature is there for a purpose which aligns with the project, it is not there for the sake of being there.  Read the project summaries that previous students have done to get an idea of what is possible and what isn't.  If you aim to get a good grade (A-range), then choose a topic that hasn't been done before.  After having a topic, start as soon as possible.  The following are specs of the development board used in the course
- Name of Board: V3 development board (野火)
- MCU on Board: STM32F103VET6
- Memory (RAM): 16 KBytes
- Flash Memory: 512 KByes
It is not necessary to use the same development board for the project.  However, your custom board should be of STM32 variant, and cannot be Raspberry Pi and Arduino :), obviously.  In addition, justification is needed for the new board.

I think I should warn you that a good topic often means complex in design.  Think of how you will achieve your project carefully.  Make sure you keep a record of what is needed to ease your shopping.

The course will only provide you with the necessary components to complete the labs.  All project components are NOT provided.  You are expected to buy them yourself.  So buckle up and start shopping at TaoBao 淘寶 or JD 京東 and do so fast, stuff takes time to be delivered.  The course will provide each person with HKD 120 reimbursement for project components (so HKD 240 per group).  For a good project, this amount is hardly enough.  For my project, my teammate and I have spent at least HKD 700 on it (before reimbursement).  So be prepared to gamble -- spending a lot doesn't mean a good grade, but often implies one.

For the final presentation, my team given them a quick overview of what the project is about and what protocols or knowledge we have used.  The rest of the presentation was providing justifications on why we have done it this way.

Last but not least, make sure your project is functional and operational for the final demo.  Please do not overestimate your ability when taking this course.  More often than not, unexpected issues arises and you will be spending 1-3 days debugging and fixing the issue.  So make sure you plan ahead and start working as soon as possible, use weekends and holidays to actually work on the project.

Side note:
Although the course officially uses C Language, the STM32F103VET6 actually supports C++.  If your project requires C++, rather than C, feel free to use it.  As usual, provide justification as to why.  Also note that using C++ instead of C adds complexity to the coding part, so be prepared for a lot of bugs :)

Wow... Now you should know why literally every student who took ELEC 3300 is complaining about the workload.  I have spent 3 days and 2 consecutive sleepless nights at HKUST right before the final demo.

Wish you best of luck for this brutal course, comrade! O7.

sections.content:
Got some dream IoT gadget or a fun toy idea? This might be the place to start building it.

There'll 6 labs to complete, 1 interim (midterm) demo, 1 final demo. Attendance is marked by IPRS.

The labs can be done at home. You just come to lab to demo or ask questions.

For the project, you're limited to the STM family of boards. They provide a development kit complete with an STM32F103 board, ST-Link, touchscreen LCD, simple sensors, a servo, pins for I2C/SPI, pins for a WiFi module, pins for a camera, and whatnot. (See attachment.)

Content:
• Introduction and Overview of Embedded Systems
• Review of Low-Level Computing (COMP2611 review)
• LCD, FSMC
    - Useful for displays/interaction
• Interrupts
    - Useful if your device doesn't need to run all the time or if you have something special to trigger
• Timers, PWM
    - Useful for regular signals, interrupts
• ADC/DAC (Analog-to-Digital Conversion and vice versa), Motors
    - Useful for analog sensors, motors, audio
• Serial Communication (UART, USB, SPI, Zigbee)
    - Useful for communicating w/ sensors/devices/computers
• DMA
    - Useful for performance

Other things you might be able to pick up:
 • Reading signal diagrams
• Hunting info in datasheets
• Googling
• Screaming in pain at 2am

All in all, it's pretty ambitious for an intro to embedded systems.

----

Some experience sharing.

Like with most courses, you'll get more out if you enter with some  fundamentals. I entered with some robotics experience (so I guess my review doesn't speak for everyone). Of course I don't know everything, there were still a lot of new things that I picked up from this course.

Our group started planning for the course before the semester started. I wanted to make something music related, so we decided on making a MIDI keyboard of sorts.

We decided to forgo the F1 board and chose an F4 board. (Unless you have an EE groupmate, I suggest not taking this approach, as you'll likely be soldering things, designing the PCB, etc.) But we went for an F4 for speed and memory.

We also used C++. Slightly more flexible on the generics/container side of things. It might be possible to do it in Rust. Maybe a bit risky though, portability of libraries and all that.
sections.teaching:
Bittersweet?

Tim Woo and Fox are both passionate instructors. Tim Woo uses good analogies. He does show some videos in the first few weeks, but these are mostly inspirational rather than contentful. The IPRS is not too bad. It tries to get you to think and dig into the details.

Some topics were rushed though. And the slides are rather messy, so it's a bit hard to find info.

You can tell Fox is rather passionate about teaching, and he guides the TAs well. The rubrics seem thorough, detailed, and fair, but it might be a bit overthought. In the end, it's up to human TAs who might have very different opinions. Nonetheless, they do put a lot of effort into explaining the rubric, giving past examples, etc.

Tutorials are skippable, but are useful for setting up things and gaining a detailed understanding. E.g. why might the ADC rate be slower when we set a higher clock rate?

TAs shared their projects and experience in the last few weeks. I completely skipped these lectures (bc 9am), but I guess they could be eye-opening if you're invested into the field.
sections.grading:
Most of your grades will come from the project. Project criteria are: complexity, design, originality, completeness, presentation. (See attachment.)

I think grading for the (final) project was okay? At least for us. Again, a lot depends on the TAs. Some have high expectations. Some have none.

The interim demo grades were very weird. Most groups I know (including mine) got around half the marks. What do the TAs expect? A fully functional product? ...four weeks into the project? ...during midterms???

I skipped a bunch of IPRS towards the end. (Who wants to get up at 9am just to be interrupted (haha!) by IPRS?)

In the end, I managed to pull an A range, which was okay considering the effort I put into the project minus the missed IPRS and the unreasonable interim grading.
sections.workload:
Not gonna lie, ELEC3300 bears comparatively high workload to other courses, but this is natural when it comes to being a hands-on/project-based course. Add to this the nature of hardware and software (bugs!). And the chance of grouping with a freerider.

Bugs are the most painful part of the project. There are software bugs. And then there are hardware bugs. If a bug persists for a while, what I would do is: (1) ask experts (e.g. Fox, online forums such as stackexchange), (2) ask other groups (esp. those who have similar projects).

To give an example, I had an issue with speakers. Emailed Fox; vague response. Asked in http://DSP.SE; got some answer about psychoacoustics. 🤷‍♂️ Eventually I was able to resolve an issue with speakers in my project by asking another group what they used for speakers and how they handled them. Apparently the hardware design was simpler than we thought.

As mentioned above, some lecture materials were rushed through. Truth be told, you can get away with not knowing, especially if the topic is not used in lab or in your project. Otherwise, you'll need to self-study to catch up.

This semester they allowed us to form groups of 3. (Previously it was only groups of 2.) I found my groupmate early on and we already had most things planned by early September (a week into Fall?). Fortunately, my groupmate shared a decent chunk of responsibility, so we ended up with a finished product.

I guess my takeaways here are: don't underestimate the workload, find good groupmate(s), communicate well, and don't be afraid to seek help.

Also: set achievable targets.

This course is designed to teach techniques on how to integrate machine-level software and
hardware in ARM-core microcontroller based systems. It makes use of industry-standard
techniques and technologies, from which students can interface, design and program
microcontroller systems. The task of the course will be to complete six laboratory experiments
which address different aspects of hardware/software interfacing, and one large

sections.content:
Basic embedded system knowledge. Like what is gpio, interrupt, timer, adc, clock, hardware communication protocols like uart, i2c, spi, etc. We use STM32F103 as the development board in labs compulsorily and project optionally. They will lend you the hardware components.

You must need to have decent C programming knowledge before enrolling this course because you will always need to use C programming in assignments, labs and project. They won't teach you C programming and assume that you know them very well. In lectures and tutorials they will only teach you theoretical concepts of embedded system.

This course has a final project. 1-2 students per group is expected. The project asks you to design a microcontroller embedded system project. You can search elec3300 in Youtube to find out the projects people did before. They will also provide some project description in previous semesters. You need to buy the required components yourself.

The concepts in this course are pretty basic if you want to do anything related to microcontroller.
sections.teaching:
Professor Vinod left UST after 6 lectures. Prof Woo taught the rest of lectures. Both of them explained concepts clearly.

TA Fox also is a great teacher. He would teach you concepts and methods that are needed in the coming lab. You need to attend the tutorial if you want to know what to do in the next lab because the progress of lecture was often slower than the lab.
sections.grading:
in-class IPRS 8%, didn't release, maybe I got ~7%
2 assignments 10%, I got 9.7%
6 labs 18%, I missed one lab so I got 15/18
1 preliminary proposal discussion 4%, didn't release, maybe I got 4%
1 proposal presentation, I got 3.65%.
1 interim project demo 9%, didn't release, maybe I got ~5%
1 final project demo 40%, I got 22/40 so 22%, mean 19.727, sd 5.013
1 final report 5%, not sure, maybe 5%

Overall I think I got ~71%, and I got B-.
It is hard to get high marks in the final project so it is hard to get A range. I think the reason why we couldn't get high marks is that I didn't apply all concepts I learnt from lab into the project. For example we didn't use timer and i2c. Our project was also not very outstanding and creative so maybe it couldn't give a good impression. Besides, since this is online semester we need to take a video demo instead of live demo. The video has length limit(<7mins) including showing the working functions and ppt presentation. Therefore the time was very limited and we couldn't show the working functions of our project very clearly. Overall too much uncertainty in the final demo that affects your marks.

Thus if you want good grade easily or you are not very into embedded system and this is not a compulsary course, you should avoid this course.

But overall fair grading.

Basic introduction to microcontrollers, just teaching you how to use the various functions and protocols on the STM32 and how to read datasheets. You only have lectures for the first half of the semester. With the assessment, this course is VERY much a hands-on course, so it is quite meaningful.
sections.teaching:
Great teaching, professor Woo and professor Vinod both go over the concepts clearly. Classes are pretty interactive with the IPRS questions. They are also both very responsive to questions in class, feel free to ask for clarification.

As with most ELEC courses, the TAs are amazing. Fox goes over what you need to do in the labs and the related concepts very clearly, he also sends us emails quite often, reminding us of deadlines and such.
sections.grading:
Quite a lot of things, but NO EXAMS! The main thing is the project, with 2-people groups. A good tip for the project: make sure it has a lot of hardware components, the graders do not care much for software.

In-class activities (8%): IPRS questions in class, 6% is given if you answer all questions, and another 2% is given if you get more than 70% of questions right. The questions are not hard, however you need to pay attention in class, otherwise you won't be able to answer them. I got all 8% I believe.

2 assignments (10%, 5% each): Pretty simple questions, just making sure you understand the lecture materials. Almost everyone has full marks on this.

6 Lab experiments (18%, 3% each): Follow the lab manual and demo the circuit and code to the TAs, quite useful as you will do similar things for the final project, difficulty is low other than the last lab. Most people have at least 15/18% since the first 5 labs are quite easy.

Preliminary proposal discussion (4%): Meet with other students in a Zoom meeting and discuss the projects you will be making, and then write a short comment on iPeer. Just submitting it will give you all 4%.

Proposal presentation (6%): Make a video presenting the project idea. Points are given based on the complexity of the project. My presentation was quite bad so I got 3% or so possibly.

Interim project demo (9%): Show the TAs and professors your current progress in the demo, you are also allowed to ask them questions on the project for feedback. Grading is completely unknown, but I think we did alright.

Final project demo and presentation (40%): Make a 7 minute video demonstrating your project and then also explain the flow of the code. After the video the TAs and professors will ask you questions on the project. (Average score: 19.7, SD: 5.01)

Final report (5%): Make a HTML file storing everything in the project, just linking everything you have already done on it. Again grading is unknown.

Nothing is shown other than my grade for the 2 assignments and the final score, with 3.5/40 higher than the average I got a B. Decent? Really unsure.
sections.workload:
VERY heavy.

No matter what you are doing for the project, you will spent a LOT of time debugging and trying to solve technical issues, some of which will have NO ANSWERS online, meaning that you really have to solve them yourself. (For example, I searched for a VERY long time for a library and could not find it, I only managed to solve it by bruteforcing what I wanted instead of an elegant solution.)

Depending on the ability of your groupmate, the workload also varies, but again, it is heavy no matter what.

(This is the start of the official description)
"This course is designed to teach techniques on how to integrate machine-level software and hardware in ARM-core microcontroller based systems. It makes use of industry-standard techniques and technologies, from which students can interface, design and program microcontroller systems. The task of the course will be to complete five laboratory experiments which address different aspects of hardware/software interfacing, and one large microprocessor/microcontroller based project which should result in the design and implementation of a small working embedded system."
This has been the official description of this course. In terms of courses provided by ECE, it really is a strange course:
1. It is the only 3000-level ELEC course that accepts a higher level COMP course (COMP2611) as a prerequisite.
2. It is a major required course only in BEng(CPEG), but not in BEng(ELEC) in which ELEC3300 is an optional course.
3. The TA of this course (Fox) is one of the important figures of CPEG Program Office. (Hope I didn't misuse the word "figure" :) )
Therefore I gave it a nickname course code: CPEG3010 :)
BTW, I love its content and it really gives me a glimpse on the industry.

sections.teaching:
Lectures are honestly boring. However, it does give you a good grasp of the fundamental concepts in data communications. If there is a real-time graded written assessment (i.e. midterm or final for some reason), understanding of these materials is pivotal for a decent course grade.

Tutorials are very informative. They kind of teach practical skillset for handling physical devices. Sometimes attending tutorials make your life easier when trying to figure out the solution for the lab exercise.

Labs are the practice part. Generally, you will be given a set of coding exercises/problems beforehand. You will need to demo your solution in lab time. Getting the correct solution requires much effort in some cases and it may take you a considerable amount of time. Here is the place where you will realize that life is much crueler than you thought, and your code can when you least suspect. Sometimes asking TAs and student helpers may make your life easier, sometimes not, especially if your coding approach is just completely wrong.

It is kind of the nature of programming-based assessments. Programming experience, knowledge of the language, coding styles etc. all comes into play. I had been a student helper for other courses as well, and I fully understand that sometimes other's code may just be weird. It can be something that I just cannot wrap my head around. It is reasonable that TAs just unable to pull you out of the hole that you, unfortunately, dug yourself into, and this is important to bear in mind.
sections.grading:
I split the grade composition into 2 parts.
Part 1:
In-class activities (iPRS): 7% + minor bonus
Homework: 4% x2
Lab task: 3% x7
Peer discussion for the final project proposal: 4%
Online presentation for the final project: 6%

Part 1 carries a total of 46%. Here is where things start to get interesting. Due to special circumstances (premature end of school term), an option is given to take final exam instead of continuing the final project. Therefore in part 2 of the composition:

Option 1:
Interim demo: 9%
Project demo + presentation: 40%
Report: 5%

Option 2:
Online final exam: 54%

(Sidenote: P/F or W were also available. Almost everyone are eligible to pass.)

I took the final exam, and I would urge you to not do the same.
Score: 153.5/180; Mean: 85.17; SD: 25.14

The mean is below 50%. The exam material covered al lot of the concepts taught within the course lecture (probably with the exception to direct memory access). It requires you to code from scratch. For example, instead of using HAL library for SPI communication (note: this is what people called bit-banging, now go look it up), we were required to implement helper functions to do the same thing ourselves with the aid of a timing diagram. One VERY LONG question also requires hardware connection, choice, and design, as well as programming a communication protocol for a piece of hardware. The difficulty of the exam is insane, even unthinkable for an ELEC course. I didn't see that coming at all.

Even if you don't take my words, the score tells you everything. So please think very very carefully before you take a written test designed by Fox. It could be the funeral for your CGA.

Needless to say, I got an A+ by the end (duh.)

Finally, WELL PLAYED FOX!
sections.workload:
Here is the rundown of what you will do in ELEC3300 sessions:
Lecture: Wait for iPRS and guess your way out.
Tutorial: Pretend to know everything even if you really don't
Before lab: Now you realize tutorial notes probably had told you everything you need to know, but you don't understand the notes
Lab: Beg your lab partner, TAs or some random nerds to do everything for you cuz you suck (jk)

In all seriousness, workload primarily concentrates on the labs and practical stuff. I would say the workload is not small. Here is some breakdown of workload.

+ Much effort is needed to fully understand lab materials and complete lab tasks.

+ If you do the project (which normally you must do so), the workload really depends on the complexity. Nevertheless, learning the methodology of datasheet skimming is non-trivial.

- Assignments are pretty easy tho. This also gave a lot of false comfort for us, thinking that the final exam is going to be just as painless and simple. (Spoiler alert! It wasn't.)

* No workload if you have the luxury /s of taking the final exam. Honestly, the lab material/tutorial slides are too simple. It really won't help you much to gear up for hardcore difficulty. But cranking up your experience may help a lot, so maybe you still want to buy some chips to play with. But then you will need to spend lots of time on things that don't count towards course grade...

So in terms of painfulness, the course project makes you feel the pain gradually. The final exam gives the same, but you feel all the pain during the exam. (maybe)

sections.grading:
Course works and Grading
– In-class activities 10%
– 2 Homework assignments 8%
– 6 Laboratory experiments 18%
– 1 Preliminary proposal discussion (peer) 4%
– 1 Final proposal presentation 6%
– 1 Interim project demonstration 9%
– 1 Final project demonstration and presentation 40% (+2%)
– 1 Final report submission 5%

Those Labs are quite difficult but they are very useful for your final project.

Labs and tutorials are much more important than the lectures!

It's not difficult to get a B+ in this course if your final project is really done all by yourself !!!!
Just put all your effort on the final project

sections.content: The content covers embedded system. If you have previous knowledge in STM, this course is chill. All content are taught with STM as the example including communication protocols, GPIO and etc. Content is not heavy and there is not test or exams on the materials.
sections.teaching: Prof. Tim Woo focuses on concepts while tutorials and labs focuses on applications. It may be interesting for those who never experienced with embedded system but will be boring for those who have previous knowledge.
sections.grading: The project is the only grading subject. Innovative ideas can add points to the grade, making the project simple but fancy is the best way to achieve good grade in this course. During presentation, TAs / prof will ask technical questions so you must have full understanding on your project. There are always some robotics team members who come and grab the A-range.
sections.workload: Only the final project which u can prepare at the start of semester. Lectures, labs and tutorials only last until mid-term and you are totally free in the second-half of the semester. Just don't fail the project.

sections.content: Basic use of an embedded board
sections.teaching: Lecture is just about the basic concepts. You will learn most things from lab work. Better to type your code yourself. This would help the final project. TAs are quite helpful and you can ask any questions.
sections.grading: Depends on your project. If your project is outstanding compare with other projects, your grade will be high. Project score is given by TAs so it would be the best if you can ask for TAs' suggestion.
sections.workload: 3 homework and 1final project. Homework will affect your subgrade but they are very easy if you just refer to the lecture slide. Project can be very heavy load. You need to prepare materials yourself. Also there will be a presentation before you start your project. It is important.

sections.content: This course teach you the basic of using the STM32. If you are not familiar with c, don't reg this course. You will bring trouble to yourself and your project partner.
sections.teaching: Sorry I only attend the first lecture so i can't command on the teaching of prof. Woo. (i am really sorry professor) However, I attended all the tutorials and Fox's powerpoint and teaching are quite clear and to the point.
sections.grading: I belief the grading is really good. I forgot to hand in the peer evaluation homework and still not dead.
sections.workload: Workload varies on the level of difficulty of your self-proposed project and the usefulness of your project partner. The schedule of the self-proposed project is a bit too tight in my opinion. Other things such as assignments are quite easy.

sections.content: Basically this course is all about STM32 microcontroller. It uses stm32f1 series microcontroller as an example, introducing many aspects of an embedded system. There are no exams and the core of this course is a self-proposed project. During this course you'll get rich hands-on experience that other elec courses might not give you.
sections.teaching: Prof. Tim Woo and TA (Fox)'s teaching is quite clear, especially Fox. His tutorials are very useful. If you attend all the tutorial sessions, lab work will be quite easy to finish(even if you skipped all the lectures).
sections.grading: This course has no midterm or final exams. 3 homework assignments and several lab sessions have a weight around 36% of the overall score but almost everyone can be able to get full marks in these two parts. So honestly speaking, the project's quality determines your grade.
sections.workload: My partner and I spent quite a lot of time on doing our projects. But it really depends on yourself. A complicated project means heavy workload and a good final grade (most likely) and vise versa. Comparing to the project,  other parts' workload can be ignored at all.
